name: human_photopic_csf
citation: Campbell, F. W., & Robson, J. G. (1968). Application of Fourier analysis to the visibility of gratings. The Journal of Physiology, 197(3), 551-566. https://doi.org/10.1113/jphysiol.1968.sp008574
human_paradigm: grating detection (report the presence/orientation of a sinusoidal luminance grating at threshold contrast)
paradigm_caveat: The human curve measures DETECTION of a low-level grating pattern; the model curve measures argmax object CLASSIFICATION correctness. These are different observer paradigms (detection vs. identification) on different stimuli, sharing a contrast axis for comparison, not identical tasks. A model threshold above or below the human curve is a difference in what each observer needs to do its own task, not proof the model 'sees like' or 'unlike' a human. Contrast metric also differs (Michelson grating vs. the model dataset's metric).
source_note: Representative photopic (light-adapted) human contrast sensitivity function for sinusoidal luminance gratings, APPROXIMATE values digitized from the canonical band-pass CSF shape reported by Campbell & Robson (1968) and consistent with the ModelFest / standard-observer literature (Watson & Ahumada, 2005; Barten, 1999). Contrast is MICHELSON contrast of a grating; sensitivity is 1 / (Michelson contrast threshold). These are reference values for illustration and cross-checking, NOT raw trial data, and NOT a substitute for measuring your own observers. The band-pass peak is near 3-5 cycles/degree with an acuity cut-off near 50-60 cycles/degree.
